campaigns.name: Alaric's march through Thrace and Greece
campaigns.strength: Gothic federates of the Frigidus campaign with families; perhaps 10,000-20,000 fighting men (modern estimates)
campaigns.summary: After revolting in 395 the Goths threatened Constantinople, moved through Macedonia and Thessaly, passed Thermopylae, extorted terms from Athens, sacked Corinth, Argos and Sparta, escaped Stilicho's blockade at Pholoe and crossed into Epirus.

path.note: Goths ravage Thrace and threaten the capital

path.t: Crossing of the Gulf of Corinth

path.note: Alaric made magister militum per Illyricum by Constantinople

campaigns.note: The order of sacks and the route are reconstructed mainly from Zosimus 5.5-7 and Claudian; exact itinerary uncertain.

campaigns.name: Alaric's first invasion of Italy
campaigns.strength: Gothic army with families, perhaps 15,000-20,000 warriors
campaigns.summary: From Illyricum Alaric crossed the Julian Alps in November 401, besieged Aquileia, cut Honorius off in Milan and Hasta, was fought to a standstill at Pollentia on Easter Day 402 and defeated near Verona, then withdrew east.
campaigns.note: Claudian's poems are the main source; the date of Verona (402 or 403) is disputed.

campaigns.name: Radagaisus's invasion of Italy
campaigns.strength: perhaps 20,000 warriors plus families (ancient figures of 200,000-400,000 are fantasy)
campaigns.summary: Radagaisus's host came from the middle Danube through Pannonia and over the Julian Alps, crossed the Po valley and the Apennines, and besieged Florence before being trapped and destroyed at Faesulae.
campaigns.note: Route unattested in detail; entry by the Julian Alps is the likeliest reconstruction.

campaigns.name: Alaric's second invasion and the sack of Rome
campaigns.strength: Gothic army swollen by c. 30,000 defectors from Stilicho's federates (Zosimus) and fugitive slaves
campaigns.summary: After Stilicho's execution Alaric marched from Noricum through Aquileia, Cremona, Bononia and Ariminum, down the Flaminia to Rome, which he blockaded in 408 and 409, seized Portus, negotiated at Ariminum, and finally sacked Rome in August 410 before marching south toward Africa.

path.note: town saved, Zosimus says, by a thunderstorm

campaigns.note: Itinerary from Zosimus 5.37 and 6.6-13 and Olympiodorus; the Ariminum-Rome shuttles are simplified.

campaigns.name: Vandal and Alan migration from the Rhine to Carthage
campaigns.strength: Hasdings, Silings and Alans; 80,000 people in 429 (Victor of Vita)
campaigns.summary: From the Rhine crossing at the end of 406 the Vandals and Alans plundered Gaul for three years, crossed the Pyrenees in 409, settled in Gallaecia and Baetica, crossed to Africa in 429 and marched east along the Mauretanian and Numidian coast to Hippo and finally Carthage.
campaigns.note: Gallic and Spanish movements are largely reconstructed from Jerome, Hydatius and Salvian; the land route through Mauretania is assumed to follow the coastal road. Gaiseric led only from 428.

campaigns.name: The Goths from Italy to Aquitaine
campaigns.strength: the whole Gothic people under Athaulf, then Wallia
campaigns.summary: After Alaric's death the Goths moved north through Italy into Gaul (412), supported and then betrayed the usurper Jovinus, took Narbonne and Bordeaux, were blockaded into Spain (415), fought the Vandals and Alans for Rome (416-418) and were settled in Aquitaine.
campaigns.note: Route into Gaul uncertain (coastal road or Alpine pass); Spanish campaigns reconstructed from Hydatius.

campaigns.name: Attila's invasion of Gaul
campaigns.strength: Huns with Ostrogoths, Gepids, Rugii, Sciri, Heruli and others; Jordanes's 500,000 is impossible, perhaps 30,000-50,000
campaigns.summary: Attila led his coalition up the Danube, crossed the Rhine in early spring, sacked Metz on 7 April, besieged Orléans until relieved by Aetius and Theodoric in June, and fought the battle of the Catalaunian Plains before withdrawing across the Rhine.
campaigns.note: Route to the Rhine and crossing point unknown; Reims and Troyes appear in hagiographic traditions (Nicasius, Lupus). Battle site disputed.

campaigns.name: Attila's invasion of Italy
campaigns.strength: main Hunnic army and subject peoples
campaigns.summary: Attila crossed the Julian Alps, destroyed Aquileia after a long siege, took the cities of the Po valley as far as Milan and Pavia, met Pope Leo's embassy on the Mincio, and withdrew amid famine and disease.
campaigns.note: Cities taken are listed by later sources; the order is reconstructed.

campaigns.name: Gaiseric's expedition against Rome
campaigns.strength: Vandal and Moorish fleet and army
campaigns.summary: Gaiseric sailed from Carthage in May 455, landed at Portus, entered Rome on 2 June after Petronius Maximus's death, plundered it for fourteen days and returned to Carthage with the empress, her daughters and the treasure of the imperial palace.
campaigns.note: Sea route schematic.

campaigns.name: Majorian's campaigns in Gaul and Spain
campaigns.strength: Italian field army with Hunnic, Gepid, Ostrogothic, Rugian, Burgundian and Suevic contingents (Sidonius); fleet of c. 300 ships
campaigns.summary: Majorian crossed the Alps in winter 458, recovered Lyon, forced the Visigoths back to alliance near Arles, marched into Spain in 460 to embark for Africa from the south-east coast, saw his fleet destroyed, and returned through Gaul to Italy, where Ricimer arrested and executed him.

path.t: Crossing the Cottian Alps in winter

path.note: attested at Zaragoza by the Chronicle of Zaragoza

campaigns.note: The Spanish leg is reconstructed from Hydatius and the Chronicle of Zaragoza.

campaigns.name: The great expedition against the Vandals
campaigns.strength: over 1,000 ships and perhaps tens of thousands of men (later sources: 1,113 ships, 100,000 men); cost 64,000-65,000 lbs of gold and 700,000 lbs of silver
campaigns.summary: Basiliscus sailed from Constantinople through the Aegean and round the Peloponnese to Sicily and then to Cape Bon, where Vandal fireships destroyed half his fleet. Parallel forces under Marcellinus took Sardinia and under Heraclius of Edessa took Tripolitania.
campaigns.note: Route schematic; the stop in Sicily is attested for the survivors.

campaigns.name: Theodoric's march to Italy
campaigns.strength: a whole people, perhaps 100,000 including 20,000 warriors, with wagons; joined by Rugians
campaigns.summary: Commissioned by Zeno, Theodoric left Novae in autumn 488, marched up the Danube, fought the Gepids at the Ulca near Sirmium, crossed into Italy, and defeated Odoacer on the Isonzo, at Verona and on the Adda before besieging him in Ravenna for two and a half years.

path.t: Sirmium: battle with the Gepids at the Ulca

campaigns.note: The route from Novae to Sirmium followed the Danube road; winter marching conditions were severe according to Ennodius.

campaigns.name: Clovis's campaign against the Visigoths
campaigns.strength: Frankish army with Burgundian contingent under Gundobad's son Sigismund
campaigns.summary: Clovis marched from Paris to Tours, crossed the Vienne at a ford revealed, Gregory says, by a stag, defeated and killed Alaric II at Vouillé, wintered at Bordeaux, seized the Visigothic treasure at Toulouse, and returned to Tours for his consular ceremony.
campaigns.note: Gregory of Tours 2.37-38 is the only narrative; Angoulême's capture may belong to 508.

campaigns.name: Belisarius's expedition to Africa
campaigns.strength: 10,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry, 500 transports, 92 dromons (Procopius 3.11)
campaigns.summary: Belisarius sailed from Constantinople around midsummer 533 via Abydos, Methone, Zacynthus and Sicily, landed at Caput Vada, marched up the coast road, won at Ad Decimum and entered Carthage, won again at Tricamarum and pursued Gelimer into Numidia.
campaigns.note: Procopius, an eyewitness, gives the itinerary in Wars 3.12-4.7.

campaigns.name: Belisarius's conquest of Sicily and Italy
campaigns.strength: 7,500 men at the start (4,000 regulars and federates, 3,000 Isaurians, plus Huns, Moors and 200 bucellarii), later reinforced
campaigns.summary: Belisarius took Sicily in 535, crossed to Rhegium, took Naples by an aqueduct, entered Rome, withstood a year-long siege, then advanced up the Adriatic side, relieved Ariminum, took Auximum and accepted the surrender of Ravenna in 540.

path.note: taken with archers hoisted to the mastheads

campaigns.note: From Procopius, Wars 5-6; movements in 538-539 simplified.

campaigns.name: Khosrow I's invasion of Syria
campaigns.strength: Persian royal army
campaigns.summary: Khosrow marched up the Euphrates, burned Sura, ransomed Hierapolis and Beroea, sacked Antioch, bathed in the Mediterranean at Seleucia, visited Apamea and Chalcis, extorted money from Edessa and Dara on the way home and settled the deportees near Ctesiphon.
campaigns.note: From Procopius, Wars 2.5-14.

campaigns.name: Narses's campaign in Italy
campaigns.strength: perhaps 20,000-30,000, including 5,500 Lombards, 3,000 Heruli, Gepids, Huns and Persian deserters
campaigns.summary: Narses marched overland from Salona round the head of the Adriatic, crossed the lagoons to Ravenna using boats and causeways, took the Via Flaminia, destroyed Totila at Busta Gallorum, retook Rome, defeated Teia at Mons Lactarius, besieged Cumae and annihilated the Franks on the Volturnus.
campaigns.note: From Procopius, Wars 8.26-35, and Agathias 1-2.

campaigns.name: The Lombard migration into Italy
campaigns.strength: Lombards with Saxons, Gepids, Bulgars and others; perhaps 100,000-150,000 people
campaigns.summary: Leaving Pannonia to the Avars on Easter Monday 568, the Lombards crossed the Julian Alps to Forum Iulii, spread across Venetia, took Milan in 569 and Pavia after a three-year siege.
campaigns.note: From Paul the Deacon 2.7-28.

campaigns.name: Priscus's campaign against the Avars
campaigns.strength: Balkan field army
campaigns.summary: Priscus crossed the Danube at Viminacium, won a series of battles against the Avars, then struck north into the Tisza region, destroying settlements and taking thousands of captives.
campaigns.note: Theophylact 8.2-4; locations north of the Danube are approximate.

campaigns.name: Shahrbaraz's conquest of Syria, Palestine and Egypt
campaigns.strength: Persian field army
campaigns.summary: After defeating Heraclius near Antioch, Shahrbaraz took Damascus, received the submission of Caesarea, stormed Jerusalem in 614 and carried off the True Cross, then invaded Egypt (618) and took Alexandria (619).
campaigns.note: Sequence certain, route and intermediate dates approximate; Shahrbaraz's command of the Egyptian campaign is inferred from later sources.

campaigns.name: Heraclius's Persian campaigns
campaigns.strength: perhaps 20,000-50,000; reinforced by up to 40,000 Turks in 627 (Theophanes)
campaigns.summary: In six years Heraclius trained an army in Anatolia, struck through Armenia into Atropatene to destroy the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp, manoeuvred against three Persian armies, fought at the Sarus, allied with the Western Turks, and in winter 627 marched into Mesopotamia to win at Nineveh, plunder Dastagird and force Khosrow's fall.
campaigns.note: Reconstructed from Theophanes, George of Pisidia, Movses Daskhurantsi and the Chronicon Paschale; the 622 battle site, the 625 manoeuvres and Ganzak's location are uncertain. See Howard-Johnston for alternative chronologies.

campaigns.name: Khalid ibn al-Walid's march to Syria and the conquest of Syria
campaigns.strength: 500-800 men on the desert crossing (tradition); Arab armies in Syria perhaps 20,000-40,000 by 636
campaigns.summary: Khalid crossed the desert from Iraq to Syria in early 634, appeared at Marj Rahit, took Bosra, joined the other armies at Ajnadayn, besieged Damascus, fought at Fahl, took Emesa, and fell back before Heraclius's great army to the Yarmuk, where it was destroyed.

path.t: Suwa, after the waterless crossing (location uncertain)

campaigns.note: The desert route has at least four variants in the Arabic tradition (Donner); dates follow the commonest traditional chronology.

campaigns.name: Amr ibn al-As's conquest of Egypt
campaigns.strength: c. 4,000 at the start, 12,000-15,000 after reinforcements
campaigns.summary: Amr entered Egypt in December 639, took Pelusium and Bilbays, won at Heliopolis with al-Zubayr's reinforcements, besieged and took the fortress of Babylon, advanced down the Delta and obtained the surrender of Alexandria by treaty in November 641.
campaigns.note: From John of Nikiu and Ibn Abd al-Hakam; dates partly reconstructed (Butler).
